😎 Happy holiday Monday! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,880 words ... 7 mins. Thanks to Erica Pandey for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

⚖️ Situational awareness: A federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration yesterday to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Get the latest.

🎤 Trump said his new press secretary, conservative commentator Katie Zacharia, starts today and will hold an introductory news conference tomorrow at 9:30 a.m. ET.
 
 
1 big thing: Beyond November
 
A harvest moon rises over Washington last fall. Photo: Kent Nishimura/Reuters

Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios.

  • Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from tomorrow if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms.

🏛️ The new analysis by FGS, a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections.

  • FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty.
  • "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says.

Zoom in: Mike Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness."

  • "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality."
Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images

Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns.

  1. "Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business."
  2. "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue."
  3. "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style."

The bottom line: "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman told me. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty."

2. Trump expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
 
President Trump walks to the White House after Marine One landed on the South Lawn on Saturday. Photo: Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images

President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, Axios' Marc Caputo reports from conversations with four people who have spoken with the president.

  • Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the Pentagon plan from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said.

Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios, that a livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen."

  • "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think."
  • An administration official told Caputo: "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this ... But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do."

Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He'd be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed.

  • The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally. In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions.

At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening.

  • Later that night, Trump was more nuanced: "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision."
  • On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters at the White House that he'll have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision."

3. 🦾 The AI gods
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Axios CEO Jim VandeHei writes in his weekly C-Suite newsletter:

Kevin Roose's new book, "The AGI Chronicles," provides a Rosetta Stone to understanding the three most important architects of modern AI: Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis.

  • Why it matters: Knowing what motivates each man helps explain their business strategies, public posturing and conflicts.

Here's my distillation of Roose's take based on his book, interviews and podcast appearances — especially Derek Thompson's Plain English, which explores the three men and their motivations.

  • Read the book. ... Listen to the pod.

⚠️ The survivalist: Dario Amodei (Anthropic)

You can trace Dario's warnings (and obsessive worry) about AI catastrophe to ... the atomic bomb. He used to hand every new Anthropic employee his favorite book, "The Making of the Atomic Bomb."

  • His hero is Leo Szilard. Szilard conceived the nuclear chain reaction and then urged fellow physicists to keep it secret. He drafted the 1939 Einstein letter to FDR that launched the Manhattan Project, then fought to restrain the bomb's use.
  • Dario has likened himself to Szilard, who decided once the blueprint of nuclear weapons was known, America had no choice but to build or control it — or lose to Nazi Germany.

Read him as: a man who believes he's building the bomb and must get there before the reckless do. It's unclear if "the reckless" is China or Sam, whom he deeply distrusts.

💸 The seller: Sam Altman (OpenAI)

Sam has two distinct gifts, in Roose's telling: an ability to sell anyone on anything and an unshakable belief in limitless scaling.

  • Altman can figure out what someone wants and give it to them, or appear to. The rap from countless former colleagues: He tells different people different things, leaving people wondering what sits at his core.
  • This has allowed him to raise insane amounts of money, turn a nonprofit into an IPO-bound behemoth and scale faster than almost anyone. It has also left Dario, Elon Musk and many former colleagues loathing him.

Read him as: the biggest, fastest, at almost any cost. Great for speed. But the purpose is the mystery.

🧪 The scientist: Demis Hassabis (Google DeepMind)

Demis got the science right — early. His AlphaFold cracked protein folding and won him a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. ("The Thinking Game" documentary is a must-watch on this.)

  • But he got LLMs wrong. He thought that modern AI would be developed in a lab governed by scientists and global leaders and shown to the public only when big problems were solved.
  • He was deeply skeptical of the scaling laws Sam and Dario rode to power — and to substantial early leads. Selling DeepMind to Google suffocated him, so Demis is scrambling to recapture his magic and glory.

Read him as: a scientist and purist forced to sprint in a race he didn't want, on a path he doubted, against two men with a big head start.

4. 💰 Post-pandemic surprise
 
Data: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

A surprising finding from one of the most thorough datasets on American household finances, released Friday morning by the Fed:

  • Middle- and lower-earners' inflation-adjusted incomes rose during the post-pandemic years — but high earners saw their incomes fall, Axios chief economic correspondent Neil Irwin writes.

5. 🛢️ Trump's refinery-for-refinery deal
 
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky meets with President Trump on the sidelines of UNGA in Manhattan in September. Photo: Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

President Trump's announcement yesterday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official told Axios' Barak Ravid.

  • The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next.

Why it matters: Trump appears to be single-handedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now, Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants.

👀 Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided.

  • A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery, which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries.
  • Six senators, including four Republicans, have called on Trump to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.

6. 🤒 Flu comes early
 
Data: CDC. Chart: Jim Sergent/Axios

Early signs suggest flu season is starting sooner than in recent years, Axios' Carly Mallenbaum writes from CDC data.

  • Why it matters: If you're thinking about getting your flu shot, health experts suggest it's time to roll up your sleeve. It takes about two weeks after vaccination to develop immunity.

Go deeper.
 
 
7. 🇬🇷 Trump may fire Guilfoyle
 

Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle greets Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens last week. Photo: Mark Schiefelbein/AP

President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" and are considering firing U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports, backed partly by embarrassing text and Signal messages, alleging she shook down donors, AP's Matt Lee reports.

  • Guilfoyle is a former Fox News host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son, Donald Jr.

📱 The Wall Street Journal reported that just before her confirmation hearing, she offered to use her administration connections in return for payment of a $100,000 American Express bill. "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she texted, adding a prayer hands emoji and a PDF with Amex payment instructions.

  • A Saturday follow-up by the Journal is headlined, "At Davos, Kimberly Guilfoyle Boasted of Private Jet Trips, Luxury Stays: Recording captures U.S. ambassador saying Greek businessmen were paying for her travels and pleading for an invite to an event with Eric Trump."

In a statement last night, her lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.

  • The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, said: "Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction."

Get the latest.
 
 
8. 📚 1 for the road: Record book bans
 

Illustration: Axios
 

Nearly 12,000 book bans were instituted in public schools over the past year, according to a new study from PEN America, the highest total since the organization began tracking five years ago.

  • Many of the bans were in Florida and Texas, where restrictive laws have been passed. Themes of race, racism, sexuality and gender identity remain the most common reasons books are challenged.

Among the titles that appeared on PEN America's Index of School Book Bans for the first time during the 2025-26 school year: Charlotte Brontë's 19th-century classic "Jane Eyre."
